---
title: "Using the Terminal"
---

## What is the terminal?

The terminal is a text-based interface for your computer. Instead of clicking on icons, you type commands and press Enter to run them.

This might feel unfamiliar at first, especially if you are used to R with RStudio, which has a graphical interface. But the terminal is the main way bioinformaticians interact with computing clusters, and after a little practice the commands become second nature.

This page is a follow-along exercise. Work through the steps in order and run each command yourself.

{{< video https://youtu.be/TZpUua3Rg28 >}}

::: {.callout-tip}
Every command on this page is safe to run. You will not break anything by following these steps.
:::

## Open a terminal

**On macOS:** Open the **Terminal** app. Find it in Applications → Utilities, or use Spotlight: press `⌘ + Space`, type "Terminal", press Enter.

**On Windows:** Open **Windows Terminal** or **PowerShell**.

You should see a prompt that looks something like:

```text
kfloer@Kates-MacBook-Pro ~ %
```

The terminal is waiting for you to type a command. Press Enter after each command to run it.

---

## Follow-along exercise

### Step 1: Find out where you are

```bash
pwd
```

`pwd` stands for **print working directory**. It shows where you currently are in the filesystem.

**You should see something like:**

```text
/Users/kfloer
```

Your path will show your own username. This location, `/Users/your_name`, is your **home directory**, the folder that belongs to you.

---

### Step 2: Move to the Desktop

```bash
cd Desktop
```

`cd` stands for **change directory**. It moves you into a different folder.

Confirm you moved:

```bash
pwd
```

**You should see:**

```text
/Users/kfloer/Desktop
```

---

### Step 3: Create a new folder

```bash
mkdir tutorial
```

`mkdir` stands for **make directory**. This creates a new folder called `tutorial` on your Desktop. You should be able to see it appear on your Desktop.

Move into the new folder:

```bash
cd tutorial
```

Confirm your location:

```bash
pwd
```

**You should see:**

```text
/Users/kfloer/Desktop/tutorial
```

---

### Step 4: Create a text file with nano

`nano` is a simple text editor that runs inside the terminal. You will use it to write scripts on Unity. Open a new file called `notes.txt`:

```bash
nano notes.txt
```

The screen changes, you are now inside the editor. You can type normally. The bottom of the screen shows keyboard shortcuts:

```text
^O  Write Out (save)       ^X  Exit
```

The `^` symbol means `Ctrl`. So `^O` means `Ctrl + O`.

Type the following 30 lines into the editor. On macOS you can paste with `Cmd + V`:

```text
Hello, this is a terminal tutorial.
I am practicing using the command line.
The terminal is a text-based interface for my computer.
Commands are typed and run by pressing Enter.
pwd shows my current location.
cd moves me to a different folder.
mkdir creates a new folder.
nano opens a text file for editing.
cat shows the contents of a file.
head shows the first 10 lines of a file.
tail shows the last 10 lines of a file.
mv moves or renames a file.
cp copies a file.
ls lists files in a folder.
The terminal is case-sensitive.
File and folder names matter exactly.
Avoid spaces in names and use underscores instead.
Press Tab to autocomplete a file or folder name.
Press the up arrow key to repeat a previous command.
Press Ctrl+C to cancel a running command.
On Unity, the terminal is how I submit jobs.
SLURM is the job scheduler on Unity.
sbatch submits a job script to SLURM.
squeue --me shows my currently running jobs.
A scratch workspace is temporary fast storage on Unity.
Final results should be copied to /work/ before the workspace expires.
Nextflow manages each step of the RNA-seq pipeline.
Apptainer provides the software containers that the pipeline uses.
nf-core/rnaseq is the specific pipeline used in this tutorial.
The terminal is one of the most powerful tools in bioinformatics.
```

**To save:** press `Ctrl + O`, then press `Enter` to confirm the filename.

**To exit nano:** press `Ctrl + X`.

You are back at the regular terminal prompt.

---

### Step 5: Read the file

Print the entire file to the terminal:

```bash
cat notes.txt
```

All 30 lines will appear.

Show just the first 10 lines:

```bash
head notes.txt
```

Show just the last 10 lines:

```bash
tail notes.txt
```

::: {.callout-tip}
`head` and `tail` are useful when a file is very large, too large to print the whole thing at once. On Unity, log files can have thousands of lines. A quick `head` or `tail` gives you a preview without waiting for everything to scroll past.
:::

### When output won't stop: Ctrl+C vs q

You will run into two situations where a command takes over your terminal and you need to get out.

**Situation 1: `cat` on a huge file**

If you accidentally run `cat` on a very large file, thousands of lines start scrolling past and will not stop on their own. Press `Ctrl+C` to cancel the command immediately.

```bash
cat huge_log_file.txt   # thousands of lines start scrolling...
# press Ctrl+C to stop
```

`Ctrl+C` cancels whatever command is currently running. Use it any time a command is doing something and you want it to stop.

**Situation 2: a pager opens (less, man, git log)**

Some commands open an interactive viewer called a **pager** instead of dumping everything to the screen at once. You will see this with `less`, `man`, and sometimes `git log`. The pager lets you scroll up and down through the content.

To open a large file in the pager:

```bash
less notes.txt
```

Inside `less`:

- `↓` / `↑` arrow keys or `j` / `k` to scroll line by line
- `Space` to jump down a full page
- `q` to quit and return to the terminal

The key difference: if the terminal is **waiting for a command**, use `Ctrl+C`. If a **pager or interactive program** is open, use `q`.

::: {.callout-note}
A quick way to tell which situation you are in: if you can see a `:` or `(END)` at the very bottom of the screen, you are inside a pager. Press `q` to exit. If the terminal prompt (`$` or `%`) is not visible at all and output is still printing, press `Ctrl+C`.
:::

---

### Step 6: Move the file to the Desktop

Right now `notes.txt` is inside the `tutorial` folder. You can see its full path:

```bash
pwd
```

```text
/Users/kfloer/Desktop/tutorial
```

Use that full path to move the file to the Desktop:

```bash
mv ~/Desktop/tutorial/notes.txt ~/Desktop/
```

`mv` takes two arguments: where the file is now, and where you want it to go. The `~` is shorthand for your home directory, so `~/Desktop/` is the same as `/Users/kfloer/Desktop/`.

Confirm the file is gone from the `tutorial` folder:

```bash
ls ~/Desktop/tutorial/
```

The folder should be empty, no output, or a blank line.

Confirm the file is now on the Desktop:

```bash
ls ~/Desktop/
```

You should see `notes.txt` listed among your Desktop items.

---

## You are done

You have practiced the core terminal commands you will use throughout this tutorial:

| What you did | Command |
|---|---|
| Checked your location | `pwd` |
| Moved to a folder | `cd` |
| Created a folder | `mkdir` |
| Created and edited a file | `nano` |
| Printed a whole file | `cat` |
| Previewed the start of a file | `head` |
| Previewed the end of a file | `tail` |
| Moved a file | `mv` |

These same commands work on Unity. The only difference is that on Unity your home directory is `/home/your_username/` instead of `/Users/your_username/`.

---

## Understanding file paths

A path describes where a file or folder is located. There are two types:

**Absolute path**, starts from the very top of the filesystem with `/`. It always points to the same place, no matter where you currently are.

```text
/work/pi_lmangiamele_smith_edu/03_26_flut_yale_rnaseq
```

**Relative path**, starts from wherever you currently are. A single dot `.` means "here" and two dots `..` mean "one folder up".

```text
../notes.txt
```

::: {.callout-tip}
When in doubt, use absolute paths. They are harder to get wrong because they always point to the same place.
:::

---

## What is a shell script?

If you have written code in R, you already understand the idea of a script: a text file containing commands that run in order from top to bottom.

A **shell script** is exactly the same thing, except the commands are terminal commands instead of R commands. When you run a shell script, the computer reads it from top to bottom and executes each line, just like R runs a `.R` file line by line.

Shell scripts usually end with `.sh`. For example:

```bash
#!/bin/bash
module load nextflow/26.04.1
nextflow run nf-core/rnaseq -r 3.26.0 -profile test,unity
```

That is a three-line shell script. The first line (`#!/bin/bash`) tells the computer which program to use to interpret the commands, think of it like a `library()` call in R that sets up the environment. The next lines are commands you would type manually, saved so they run automatically.

The job scripts in this tutorial are shell scripts with extra lines at the top starting with `#SBATCH`. Those are instructions for SLURM, they tell the job scheduler how much time and memory to reserve. Everything else is plain terminal commands.

::: {.callout-tip}
The `.sh` extension is a convention, not a requirement. Some people name SLURM scripts `.sbatch`. Both work, the extension is just a label to remind you what the file does.
:::

## Quick command reference

| Goal | Command |
|---|---|
| See where you are | `pwd` |
| List files | `ls` |
| List files with sizes | `ls -lh` |
| Move into a folder | `cd folder_name` |
| Move up one folder | `cd ..` |
| Go to home directory | `cd ~` |
| Create a folder | `mkdir folder_name` |
| Create nested folders | `mkdir -p parent/child` |
| Create or edit a file | `nano file.txt` |
| Print a file | `cat file.txt` |
| Preview the start | `head file.txt` |
| Preview the end | `tail file.txt` |
| Watch a file update live | `tail -f file.txt` |
| Move or rename a file | `mv old new` |
| Copy a file | `cp source destination` |
| Copy a folder | `cp -r source/ destination/` |
| Check folder size | `du -sh folder/` |
| Check disk space | `df -h .` |
| Copy files to/from Unity | `scp source destination` |
| Cancel a running command | `Ctrl + C` |

## Tips for beginners

- File and folder names are **case-sensitive**. `Results` and `results` are two different folders.
- Avoid spaces in file names, use underscores `_` or hyphens `-` instead.
- Press `Tab` to autocomplete a file or folder name. Press it twice to see all matches if there are several.
- Use the `↑` arrow key to scroll back through previous commands, no need to retype.
- Read error messages carefully, they usually tell you exactly what went wrong.
- If a command seems stuck, press `Ctrl + C` to cancel it.

## Copying files between Unity and your laptop

`scp` copies files between your laptop and Unity. Run these commands **from a terminal on your laptop** (not from Unity).

Copy a file from Unity to your current folder:

```bash
scp kfloer_smith_edu@unity.rc.umass.edu:/path/to/multiqc_report.html .
```

Copy a whole folder from Unity to your laptop:

```bash
scp -r kfloer_smith_edu@unity.rc.umass.edu:/path/to/results/ .
```

Copy a file from your laptop to Unity:

```bash
scp samplesheet.csv kfloer_smith_edu@unity.rc.umass.edu:/scratch4/workspace/kfloer_smith_edu-demo/
```

The `.` at the end means "copy it here, into my current directory."

::: {.callout-note}
Replace `kfloer_smith_edu` with your own Unity username and replace the paths with your actual file paths.
:::
